bbva.intro: BBVA shows solid progress in structuring its 'Net Zero' roadmap between 2024 and 2025, evidenced by the expansion of scope towards key sectors such as Aluminium and cargo Aviation. However, the bank faces transparency challenges arising from methodological restatements in Oil & Gas and an alarming deviation in meeting short-term targets in its Steel portfolio.

points.title: Critical setback and lack of transparency in Steel
points.body: It is essential to focus on the 12% increase in the Steel sector's physical intensity reported in 2025 versus the previous year. This sharp rise is presented without any contextual or macroeconomic explanation in the report, undermining the credibility of the 2030 target for this heavy portfolio.

points.title: Break in the historical series in Oil & Gas due to inclusion of 'midstream'
points.body: The change to the base-year absolute emissions of the Oil & Gas portfolio (an increase of 0.6 MtCO2e) improves completeness but breaks the comparability of the progress reported in 2024, constituting a methodological risk as the ambition of the final reduction percentage was not clearly reformulated.

points.title: Impossibility of traceability in the Shipping portfolio
points.body: The adoption of the Poseidon Principles v4 as the governing framework in the 2025 report versus the previous 2024 model hinders continuous transition-risk tracking for maritime assets, requiring a bridge baseline to be established so that investors can measure shipowners' real improvement.

points.title: Strengthening by bringing forward commitments in Coal
points.body: The decision to bring forward by two years (from 2040 to 2038) the target for eliminating global thermal-coal exposure, as certified in the 2025 report's strategic update, is a highly positive signal for the market.

santander.intro:
As a final conclusion of this comparative analysis, an evolution towards flexibility and operational pragmatism is observed, at the expense of the rigidity of the initial commitments.
Banco Santander's overall evolution shows a pragmatic refocusing of its decarbonization strategy, moving away from fixed, absolute targets towards flexible intensity ranges. This adjustment, which the bank attributes to the need to reflect the real pace of transition and the dependence on public policy, mainly affects the comparability of its commitments in the most polluting sectors and denotes a loosening of the climate scenarios previously adopted.

points.title: Setback in Oil & Gas ambition
points.body:
The absolute-emissions target is removed and Scope 3 is excluded from the alignment target, shifting to a monitoring-only metric (Primary Energy Index).
Scope 3 emissions (those generated by the use of the products sold by oil companies) typically account for more than 80–90% of the sector's total impact. By moving these emissions to a "monitoring index" (Primary Energy Index) instead of a portfolio-linked reduction target, the direct pressure on clients' carbon imbalance decreases. The bank justifies this by stating that clients have "greater operational control" over their Scopes 1 and 2.

points.title: Methodological shift towards target ranges
points.body: The bank has systemically replaced its emission targets set as a strict value (whether absolute or intensity) with flexible intensity ranges (in Power, Steel, Automotive), arguing the need to absorb the different international transition speeds.

points.title: Massive update of base years
points.body:
The base years of most CIB sectors have been reset from 2019 to 2023, hindering the traceability of long-term historical progress.
Changing the base year makes it harder to compare historical progress. If a bank reduces emissions between 2019 and 2023 but then "resets" the counter in 2023, the long-term trajectory becomes fragmented. The bank argues that this change seeks to use more recent and accurate data to reflect the current composition of its portfolio.

points.title: Reclassification of hard-to-abate sectors
points.body:
The bank has given up maintaining a decarbonization target for aviation, moving it to "monitoring" citing a lack of control over the sector's levers.
This represents a loosening of the climate commitment in a hard-to-abate sector. The bank explains that, given the current size of its exposure (EUR 0.53 billion) and the total dependence on external technologies such as sustainable fuel (SAF), it does not consider it feasible to maintain a binding alignment target at this time.

points.title: Alteration of the baseline climate scenario
points.body: The institution has abandoned the exclusivity of the IEA Net Zero 2050 scenario, incorporating the less restrictive Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) into the definition of all its new sectoral target ranges.

sabadell.intro: Banco Sabadell shows overall progress in its decarbonization strategy, achieving notable intensity reductions in key sectors. When the institution's explanations are taken into account, it becomes clear that the volatility in the monitoring indicators largely reflects the high concentration of certain portfolios and temporary mismatches in the availability of client data.

points.title: Exceptional drop in the power sector
points.body: Physical intensity has plunged to 40 Kg CO2e/MWh, beating the lower bound of the target range (45–85) ahead of schedule thanks to the weight of renewable project finance.

points.title: Justified spike in oil and gas
points.body: The rise in emissions to 5,277 Kt CO2e (versus the previous 4,820 Kt CO2e) underscores the sensitivity of the absolute footprint to new one-off commercial-credit drawdowns.

points.title: Impact of concentration in aluminium and coal
points.body: The atypical rise in aluminium intensity (+9.8%) and the spike in coal exposure (from EUR 0.1m to EUR 1.7m) show that, in small or highly concentrated portfolios, working-capital lines or mix changes significantly distort the trend towards 2030.

points.title: Data lag in Shipping
points.body: The worsening of the Alignment Delta to +28% highlights the current challenges in ESG data quality, forcing the bank to use one-year lags (2023 data to estimate 2024).

points.title: Marked progress in automotive
points.body: The abrupt improvement to 183 gCO2e/vkm validates the portfolio-reallocation strategy towards automotive groups with more aggressive transition plans.

caixabank.intro: CaixaBank's overall evolution towards decarbonization shows accelerated progress in the energy sectors (Power and Oil & Gas), far exceeding the 2030 targets, but presents stagnation and even severe setbacks in sectors linked to external regulatory changes such as Automotive, or with proxy-data problems such as Commercial Real Estate. Methodologically, the baseline is consistent, although occasional numerical discrepancies surface in the historical recalculation of certain years.

points.title: Severe worsening and discrepancy in the Automotive sector
points.body: An alarming increase has been observed in the automotive sector's emissions intensity in 2025 (163.9 gCO2/vkm), exceeding even the base-year level (154 gCO2/vkm) due to regulatory loosening in Europe, compounded by a retroactive alteration of the 2023 figure with no further justification in the latest report.

points.title: Early achievement of 2030 targets
points.body: The power-generation and oil-and-gas portfolios have experienced drastic falls in their absolute metrics and physical intensities, with both standing in 2025 below the final target the bank had set out to reach within five years.

points.title: Setback in Commercial Real Estate driven by proxies
points.body: The bank reports an increase to 21 kgCO2e/m2 in its commercial real estate portfolio in 2025 that exceeds the original starting point (20.5 kgCO2e/m2), driven not by a real emissions increase but by a methodological adjustment in the estimation of proxy data given the lack of actual certificates.

points.title: Silent adjustment of historical data in Power
points.body: In cross-checking the reports, a retroactive change has been identified in the intensity figure for financial year 2022 for the power sector, moving from the 116 kgCO2e/MWh reported in 2024 to 118 kgCO2e/MWh in 2025, suggesting internal recalculations that affect the public traceability of the metric.
